## Deliverable Overview

In the spring semester before your second year, you will identify which capstone pathway you plan to pursue and will share your preferences for which workshop courses you will take in your second year. The process of adopting your capstone is described below, including the use of the capstone adoption [web form](https://forms.illinois.edu/sec/1915761140) (for all pathways) and the [capstone adoption form](files/02_CapstoneAdoption.pdf) (required in addition to the web form for all pathways).

## Capstone Pathways

There are three pathways to satisfy the practice component of the MUP capstone requirement. By default, you are expected to pursue the Plan Making Workshop pathway. Students wishing to pursue the Project Pathway or Thesis Pathway need to describe their projects in detail and petition to adopt an alternate pathway.

**Plan Making Workshop:** Exposure to professional planning practice by completing two plan making workshops. The audience for the projects completed in these workshops is typically planning and policy practitioners and decision makers. Faculty workshop leaders work in partnership with an institution, organization, or community partner to determine the scope and deliverables from the workshop in advance. Typical workshop deliverables may be a report, a plan, or other professional quality work.

**Master's Project:** A professional project or analysis focusing on a topic relevant to the student's selected concentration and career goals. The audience for a master’s project is typically planning and policy practitioners and decisionmakers. The capstone deliverable may be a report, a plan, or other professional quality work. The project is conducted for or with an external client.

**Masters Thesis:** A scholarly applied or basic research work conducted under the formal Thesis Guidelines of the Department and Graduate College. The audience for a master’s thesis is typically academic and applied researchers. The thesis option is most appropriate for MUP students with a strong interest in pursuing a research-oriented career or PhD degree.

## Pathway Documentation

One of your first tasks is to "adopt" your capstone project. You will do this in the spring before your second year by completing the [following form](https://forms.illinois.edu/sec/1915761140) to indicate your capstone pathway and preferences regarding workshop offerings.

### UP 510 Workshop Descriptions

You will have two UP 510 Plan Making Workshop courses in your second year of the program — one offered in the fall semester and one in the spring. Given the intensive nature of workshops, the department does not allow students to register for more than one UP 510 offering per semester.

You will complete the capstone adoption [web form](https://forms.illinois.edu/sec/1915761140) to share your capstone pathway. The department will then enroll you in the fall and spring workshop offerings.

Below are general descriptions of the UP 510: Plan Making Workshops being offered in Academic Year 2026-2027.

#### Retrofitting Suburbia Using Small Area Plans (Fall 2026)

**Instructor:** [Dustin Allred](https://urban.illinois.edu/people/profiles/dustin-allred-aicp/)

**Semester Offered:** Fall 2026

**Workshop External Partner:** City of Bloomington, IL

**Workshop Description:** Like many cities in the US, the central Illinois city of Bloomington is interested in seeing the site of a dying mall rehabilitated through redevelopment. The 54 acre Eastland Mall is a strategically important site east of downtown Bloomington that presents an interesting opportunity to apply planning ideas like “retrofitting suburbia” in the creation of a small area plan that describes how this site can evolve into a more sustainable, just, healthy, and community-serving place. Although the city has some ideas for what could happen on this site, it would be up to the students in the workshop to engage with key stakeholders and collect and analyze data on existing conditions to create a compelling and feasible vision for how the site could be transformed.

**Expected Outputs:** Outputs from this workshop will include a polished professional small area type plan that synthesizes stakeholder input and background information and includes a development concept, site plan and implementation strategies. Students will also be expected to present this information to decision makers at the City of Bloomington.

#### Community Engagement & Industrial Heritage Planning in Coal-Impacted Vermilion County, Illinois (Spring 2027)

**Instructor:** [Emily Guske](https://ler.illinois.edu/directory/emily-guske/)

**Semester Offered:** Spring 2027

**Workshop External Partner:** Climate Jobs Institute (CJI)

**Workshop Description:** The 2021 Climate and Equitable Jobs Act (CEJA) requires all coal-fired electrical generation power plants in Illinois to close by 2030, with few exceptions. No requirement exists for coal mine closures under CEJA, though researchers predict that mine closures will follow plant closures. In Chicagoland, Central, and Southern Illinois, many closures have already occurred or will soon occur. Closures displace workers and impact communities economically, socially, and environmentally. While some closures preceded CEJA, the state legislative deadlines ushered in a new period in Illinois’ energy transition, creating urgent questions around the future of coal communities across the state.

In Summer 2025, the Climate Jobs Institute (CJI) at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign initiated [The Illinois Coal Workers & Communities Listening Project](https://ler.illinois.edu/climate-jobs-institute/coal/), a multi-year research project aimed at investigating the impacts of coal plant and mine closures. This research engages workers and community members who’ve lived through closures — or are preparing for them now — to understand what’s happening on the ground. The Illinois Coal Workers & Communities Listening Project intends to foreground lived experiences, honor workers’ stories, inform better policy, and use lessons learned to strengthen communities shaped by the coal industry.

In this workshop sponsored by CJI, students will conduct research, community engagement, and plan-making to support The Illinois Coal Workers & Communities Listening Project. This workshop will focus on Vermilion County, located between Champaign County and the Indiana border. Vermilion County experienced a coal plant closure in 2011, and its last active coal mine closed in 2021. A thirty-minute drive from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Vermilion County possesses a rich history of coal and continues to live with its legacy. For decades, the Vermilion coal-fired power plant dumped coal ash into unlined ponds, causing arsenic, barium, boron, chromium, iron, lead, manganese, molybdenum, nickel, and sulfate to leach into the Middle Fork River and groundwater. Additionally, nearly 30 abandoned mine land sites require attention in Vermilion County.

In Fall 2025, DURP graduate students completed a semester-long project titled “Exploring Coal’s Legacy: Heritage Trail Creation in Vermilion County”. The class documented sites that tell the story of coal’s deep influence on Vermilion County’s social, environmental, and economic landscape. UP 510 students then proposed a coal heritage trail through Vermilion County. Their mapping project highlights locations that range from local museums preserving miners’ stories to fossil-rich formations in an underground petrified rainforest, as well as areas affected by coal ash contamination along the Middle Fork River. They produced a [StoryMap](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/9ce13f11c95c4313b64db849d8d7c6a7) and presented their work to the public at the Vermilion County Museum. In Spring 2027, the new cohort of students will build on the inaugural class’s research, producing an independent community-engaged project focused on planning topics like industrial heritage, collective memory, economic development, and eco-tourism.

### Additional Documentation for Projects and Theses

-   For the **Project Pathway** you need to share a detailed description of your projects subject and scope, a description of your client, and need to secure the signature of your client and the faculty member who has agreed to supervise your project. Detailed [project proposal guidelines](../guidelines/project.qmd) are available under the pathway description.

-   For the **Thesis Pathway** you need to share a project abstract and need to secure the signature of your thesis advisor and a second faculty committee member. You should have also shared a detailed proposal with both your thesis adviser and your other committee member by the time you adopt your capstone.Detailed [thesis proposal guidelines](../guidelines/thesis.qmd) are available under the pathway description.

## Milestone Deliverable

If you pursue the Workshop pathway, the only needed documentation is the submission of the pathway adoption web form in the spring of your first year, and the capstone adoption form in the fall of the second year. For those who are petitioning to adopt the project or thesis pathway, please complete the [Capstone Adoption Form](files/02_CapstoneAdoption.pdf), including all required signatures (based upon the capstone pathway you are pursuing) and including your proposal and submit to the file dropbox below.
